newsitem.title: FRANCE: Barley focus shifts to suppliers after Saudi deal.
newsitem.headline: Barley focus shifts to suppliers after Saudi deal.

text.p: Attention in the world barley market shifted to Brussels and Canada on Thursday as traders weighed up the cost of supplying 500,000 tonnes of barley to Saudi Arabia for April and May in a deal clinched on Wednesday.
Four companies were involved in the sale, traders said, with most observers estimating the price of the deal at $152 to $154 per tonne, including freight.
A detailed breakdown of prices was not available, however, and is likely to be kept under wraps, operators said.
Traders said nearby deliveries for late April went for between $153 and $154 per tonne, though some put the price for later periods as low as $150 or even $149 per tonne.

Analysts trying to evaluate the deal said they were using a calculation for freight and expenses of some $22 per tonne. This includes the cost of meeting a Saudi requirement that imported barley should be partly dyed red to separate it from local crop.
A starting point for negotiatons with Brussels over export subsidies might therefore be $130 per tonne Fob, in line with recent sales, though some exporters argued this should be lower.

The EU Commission will want to carefully study bids for Ecu-denominated refunds especially in the light of the dollar's sharp rise since last week, which should save on subsidies, a member country official said.
The European Union's most recent export refund for barley was 31.98 Ecus per tonne, issued last week.
Although the dollar shed some of its gains overnight, the U.S. currency is about three percent stronger against the French franc, for example, than it was at last Thursday's EU tender.
At the same time, however, exporters were expected to press the EU to price its barley below $130 per tonne to compete with Canadian supplies that are likely to take part of the business.
There was talk in Canada on Wednesday that the country had 150,000 tonnes to offer for the tender and one major operator was today said to be looking for freight for 50,000 tonnes.

Traders reckoned a fob European barley price of $130 per tonne would call for refunds of at least 33 Ecus per tonne this week to allow for a rise of some 3.5 percent in domestic barley. This had more than compensated for the dollar's movement.
But with currency markets still volatile, finding the right refund level this time was particularly risky, one trader said.
Using the dollar's level of one week ago, EU refunds would be worth 36 to 37 Ecus for immediate execution, traders said.
Using the current dollar but last week's refund, the fob French price would be some $131 to $132 a tonne.
Traders bid for refunds this morning ahead of the weekly EU cereals management committee meeting set for the afternoon.
EU officials have said they have plenty of barley left to sell and traders expect the bloc to get most of the Saudi deal.
